newsitem.title: USA: Alaskan panel offers hunting, fishing compromise.
newsitem.headline: Alaskan panel offers hunting, fishing compromise.

text.p: A hunting and fishing dispute between rural Alaskans and urbanites could be ended by changing the state constitution and federal and state laws, a panel said on Thursday.
The seven-member panel appointed by Gov. Tony Knowles released its plan to solve Alaska's problem with "subsistence:" traditional harvests of fish, game and wild plants for personal use.

Federal law mandates a subsistence preference for rural residents, but Alaska's constitution forbids giving different fishing and hunting rights to residents of different regions. Most of Alaska's rural population is native, while most of its city-dwellers are white.
The federal law was established under provisions of the 1980 Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, which set up vast expanses of national parks, wildlife refuges and wilderness areas.
But a 1989 Alaska Supreme Court decision, issued after urban sport hunters filed suit, scrapped the state's rural preference as a violation of the state constitution.

Since then, efforts to change the Alaska constitution to conform to federal law have stalled, and the federal government plans to take over management of fish and game on federal lands and waters in Alaska in October.
Charlie Cole, a former state attorney general and a member of the panel, said the plan offered a last chance for Alaska to retain fish and wildlife management throughout the state.

"I think we have a window of opportunity at this juncture to do that," Cole, a Republican, said at a news conference. "But I have great apprehension about this being our last opportunity if we don't act now."

Under the plan, the state constitution would be amended to permit a rural preference, while the legislature would pass new laws administering the preference and Congress would alter federal law to make state management easier.

Former Republican Gov. Jay Hammond, also on the panel, urged Alaskans to support the plan because future federal management could be as "incompetent" as it was before statehood. "Nothing's any good, unless the alternative's worse," he said.
